newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: OAU summit to close with commitment to democracy.
newsitem.headline: OAU summit to close with commitment to democracy.

text.p: Africa's annual stocktaking ends in Harare on Wednesday with most of the continent's leaders committed to democracy and economic union, but with little agreement on how either should be achieved.
The 33rd summit of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) is scheduled to end around 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) with the adoption of a final communique setting targets for the year ahead.
Democracy and further work on a 50-year plan to create an African common market by 2030 are likely to dominate the leaders' final comment on the three-day gathering.

Delegates said leaders resolved in a closed session on Tuesday to support the reconstruction of the former Zaire and the return to power of Sierra Leone's elected civilian government after a military coup on May 25.
In line with the OAU's renewed commitment to democracy, the summit supported the Nigerian-led military attack on the Sierra Leone capital of Freetown.

"We resolved to continue to support the ECOWAS (Economic Community for West African States) action in Freetown and agreed that no one would have anything to do with the council appointed by the coup-makers," one southern African delegate said.

Though an African crisis management capacity to identify and manage conflicts such as those in Zaire and Sierra Leone before they erupt was discussed in the corridors, delegates said it was not raised formally.

Delegates who declined to be named said the summit accepted the bona fides of its newest member, President Laurent Kabila of the Democratic Republic of Congo, previously Zaire, and promised him moral and active support in rebuilding his country.
Kabila was welcomed with hugs and applause at the opening session and then dozed through opening speeches that shared a common theme: Africa is ready for democracy.
But he left before his take over in Kinshasa was discussed and his foreign minister, Bizima Karaha, said the nature of the support promised by the OAU members was not spelled out.
"We need moral support, we need financial support and we need help to rebuild our infrastructure," he told Reuters after the debate. "I'm sure that is what we will get from the OAU."
Several delegates said privately that the ringing support for democracy throughout the summit must have made some of the continent's longer serving and less democratic leaders nervous.
"The general tone is that Africa is done with despots and dictators. Democracy's time has come," said one delegate.
He said Nigeria, where General Sani Abacha siezed power in a coup and earned worldwide condemnation for executing leading opponnets, would come under increasing pressure to reform.
Abacha was expected at the conference, but did not arrive.
